name: Liability When Agents Interact
title: Liability When Agents Interact
answer: This page covers legal responsibility when two or more AI agents act together or against each other without a human directing each step. It includes harm from automated negotiations, coordinated trading, autonomous vehicles, and multi-agent software that makes binding commitments. The field asks whether liability falls on the agent's developer, deployer, user, or the owner of the platform where the agents met. It also examines how traditional doctrines of agency, contract, tort, and product liability apply when no single human made the final choice.

It includes harm from automated negotiations, coordinated trading, autonomous vehicles, and multi-agent software that makes binding commitments. The field asks whether liability falls on the agent's developer, deployer, user, or the owner of the platform where the agents met. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Liability analysis depends on the technical substrate that records what each agent did. That includes agent identifiers, message logs, decision traces, model versions, prompt histories, and human approval checkpoints. Many multi-agent systems run on cloud orchestration services, API gateways, and smart contract platforms that can preserve an immutable record of interactions. Courts and regulators increasingly expect these records to show which agent initiated an action, what information it used, and whether a human could have intervened.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work of assigning liability starts with reconstructing the causal chain across agent interactions. Lawyers and technical experts review system design, training data, guardrails, delegation limits, and the terms under which each agent was authorized to act. They ask whether the harm was foreseeable, whether a human set a risky objective, and whether any agent exceeded its instructions. This analysis often relies on audit logs, model documentation, and incident reports rather than testimony about a single human decision.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on provenance, because diffuse control makes fault hard to locate. Some jurisdictions apply agency law, treating an agent as a tool of its principal, while others look to product liability or negligence for defective design or inadequate oversight. Contractual disclaimers and insurance policies may shift risk, but courts can override them where harm is serious or consumers are involved. The site tracks 6823 state AI bills, some of which propose new liability rules for autonomous systems, alongside 210 compliance and regulation pages that map existing duties.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect clearer rules for agent identity, mandatory logging, and human override requirements in high-risk settings. Courts are likely to develop multi-factor tests that weigh the degree of autonomy, the foreseeability of harm, and the quality of monitoring. Insurance markets may create new products for multi-agent failures, and regulators may impose strict liability for certain agent-to-agent transactions. The direction is toward making the chain of responsibility legible even when no single human controlled the outcome.
